positions.commentary: The speaker acknowledges that Adobe is still growing, citing 11% revenue growth in the last year.
The speaker suggests that Google's dominance in restaurant search could potentially impact food delivery, though they find that scenario far-fetched.
The speaker hopes Tesla eventually gets an autonomous vehicle taxi cab and mentions Elon Musk saying it will turn on soon.
The speaker notes CPRT's CEO Jeffrey Law was talking about IAA and saying a lot of things that didn't make sense.

thesis: The episode argues that Adobe faces significant existential risks from AI competition, citing decelerating growth, delayed price hikes, and a binary outcome where the company could become 'useless.' Conversely, Uber is viewed as a battleground stock facing destructive margin pressure from competition with autonomous vehicle firms like Waymo and Tesla, though the speaker acknowledges it will likely survive the next decade.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Adobe faces significant risks and feels there is a strong case for things to go wrong, despite its growth.
claims.quote: But it does seem like there's a pretty strong case for a lot to go wrong. So, I think people are going to have to, I think people are going to land on one side of the fence here.

claims.claim: The speaker states they do not have a strong opinion either way on Adobe and feel they are over the conversation.
claims.quote: And I think that there are better software companies that have stronger positions. And I can kind of see how that's going to not see, but I feel like I have a stronger position on where their value proposition lies in a world where, again, not a world where AI literally replaces every human who's ever existed and we're in a Wally scenario.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Uber will become a worse business in five years due to competition from autonomous vehicle companies like Waymo and Tesla.
claims.quote: In my opinion, it seems like Uber will become a worse business. Simply from the existence, first of Waymo, just being in the market at all and secondly, from Tesla, who even though they've been pretty late, I do think they're gonna eventually hit the market with a robot taxi and be able to turn on a lot of vehicles with autonomous and I think they're gonna also have their own direct app and wanna

claims.claim: The speaker is concerned that Uber will have to respond to competition with promotions, which is destructive to margins.
claims.quote: I don't see how this isn't something they don't fully play out and it doesn't weigh on Uber's profitability eventually as they have to respond with promotions of their own.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Waymo as having a better experience, being safe, and having a nicer car compared to other options.
claims.quote: I love Waymo, I think it's a better experience. I think the journey is, we'll say it's pretty safe. I mean, there's a couple of times where I go, whoa, Hey, Mo, what are you doing over there? But I haven't had any issues with it and it's just a much better experience.

claims.claim: The speaker hopes Tesla eventually gets an autonomous vehicle taxi cab and mentions Elon Musk saying it will turn on soon.
claims.quote: I mean, Tesla, I don't know, one day hopefully they get an autonomous vehicle taxi cab. I know that they're piloting some of it. Apparently that's gonna turn on in any moment according to Elon Musk and there's gonna be a huge fleet of autonomous vehicles in my Tesla.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Uber will survive in 10 years but questions if the current 20-25x valuation is justified given competitive risks and potential margin pressure.
claims.quote: But I don't know, I guess if you're asking me base case scenario I think they'll be fine. Drew, you know, I have to say you but a little more optimistic these days than you were historically.

claims.claim: The speaker worries about Uber's profitability over the next several years due to the need for promotions and a potential competitive cycle that could weigh on financial results.
claims.quote: I'm just worried about kind of the next several years for them in terms of what this means for their profitability if they have to respond in terms of promotions and all of that which I do think is gonna end up happening in a lot of their cities.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the market is pricing in declining margins or profits, assuming Uber cannot grow earnings at mid-double digits despite a rosy outlook.
claims.quote: So the market in my opinion is very much pricing in, margins going down or profits going down in the future. I don't think the market's assuming that they're gonna be able to grow earnings mid double digits, 20% plus.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that while Uber might be fine in the suburbs, Waymo could pick off big cities, and a shift to selling autonomous tech to OEMs could change the business model significantly.
claims.quote: Yeah, I do think that Uber in the suburbs is gonna continue to do much better. And so if you were to ask me like on margin what I actually think is gonna happen, I think Uber is gonna be fine.

claims.claim: The speaker questions whether investors paying 20-25 times earnings will be okay, acknowledging that while the company will likely exist in 10 years, the valuation is uncertain.
claims.quote: You know, will investors at this time paying 20, 25 times for it be okay. I guess time will tell.

claims.claim: The speaker expresses concern that a scenario where Waymo launches in new cities or teams with a private equity firm to own a fleet could have an adverse effect on Uber's business.
claims.quote: And I don't know that I would really feel that confident that that can't happen and that that it's not gonna have an adverse effect on Uber's business.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Uber faces a lot of risk and that their margins are up for debate, even if the business survives the next decade.
claims.quote: I think I've kind of laid out a lot of them and on Twitter too I've talked about a lot of those but if you're taking, you know, a 10 year time horizon do I think they're still gonna be around I think they're still gonna be around. You know, what their margins are gonna be I do think is up for debate though.

claims.claim: The speaker views Adobe as a company facing significant challenges due to AI, comparing its situation to a melting ice cube and suggesting it might be useless or face a binary outcome.
claims.quote: And it's just Adobe's kind of reminiscent of a melting ice cube to me, and I can't get over it. And again, that's just me on a 10,000-stand-foot view watching your videos on 3X speed. I can't get over that narrative.

claims.claim: The speaker believes it is challenging to see how Adobe will maintain its position in the world given the rise of AI tools.
claims.quote: I think when you talk about, and we've spoken about QuickBooks, we're going to talk about Uber, not really, you know, to an extent to software company, I think Adobe definitely more challenging to see what that world looks like.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Adobe Express is currently a free product that has gained many users and has begun monetizing some of them.
claims.quote: Adobe Express is a free product right now and has been gaining a lot of users and they've been somewhat successful at already monetizing some of those.

claims.claim: The speaker acknowledges that Adobe is still growing, citing 11% revenue growth in the last year.
claims.quote: If you're looking at, you know, revenue in the last year, it grew 11%. So, I mean, I get it, it's compelling. I mean, it is an intellectually stimulating conversation because you don't

claims.claim: Uber is mentioned as a battleground stock for the AI autonomous wave alongside Adobe.
claims.quote: And that's kind of why Adobe Uber, not really Netflix, but Adobe and Uber have kind of been battleground stocks for this AI, autonomous wave

claims.claim: The speaker personally prays for the downfall of Adobe and hates the company.
claims.quote: I personally am praying on the downfall of Adobe and, you know, that's just me. I hate them.

claims.claim: The speaker believes there are no great prospects for Adobe's business given AI competition.
claims.quote: I don't see great prospects for that business. The whole creative cloud thing, I think there's a lot more businesses that are gonna be AI native to editing photos, videos

claims.claim: Adobe's ARR has decelerated for the 10th consecutive quarter.
claims.quote: The quick update on Adobe is they had yet another quarter of ARR growth decelerating. So, their annualized recurring revenue growth has continued to decelerate. I believe this marks the 10th consecutive quarter this number has gone down.

claims.claim: Adobe is delaying price increases until after the current CEO leaves.
claims.quote: Interestingly, they're delaying it until after the current CEO leaves. So, whoever the next CEO comes in is gonna be the one to with handle that potential backlash from raising prices.

claims.claim: Adobe's stock hit lows of $190 a share and is now back up to $220.
claims.quote: The stock hit new all-time lows or maybe not all-time lows, but at least, you know, at least in the past few years all-time lows, I think it got as low as $190 a share. Now it's back up to 220 a share.

claims.claim: Adobe's multiple is 10 to 12 times cash flow earnings.
claims.quote: but it's 10 to 12 times if you're picking cash flow versus earnings multiple.

claims.claim: Adobe's CFO stepped down to go to Marvell.
claims.quote: combined with the fact that at the time, the CFO also stepped down. So, this one I didn't actually think was as big of a deal because he left to go to Marvell

claims.claim: Adobe has not disclosed the percentage of business that is consumer creativity.
claims.quote: And they've never disclosed this number. And I wonder why, because if it was a small amount and they could just put to rest the bear case, why wouldn't they just disclose that, you know, creativity revenue for consumers or total revenue from consumers is only 20% of the business.

claims.claim: Adobe resegmented their financials in a confusing way organized by product groups rather than customer groups.
claims.quote: especially because they just resegmented their entire financials and they did it in a super confusing way where they call certain segments by customer group that are not organized by customer group. They're organized by product groups.

claims.claim: Adobe's Acrobat business is a relic of the 1990s and the PDF is a standard.
claims.quote: I think they're, the PDF is a relic of the 1990s and the fact that they have been able to extract this much value out of the entire American society and most of the globe for this stupid feature that makes a word dock lockable.

claims.claim: Adobe's Acrobat UI feels very locked and is hard to use.
claims.quote: Having said that, I'm probably not gonna deal with an alternative. So, I mean, if you give me an alternative that lets me edit a PDF that's not Adobe, I will. Yeah, they're out there, they're out there.

claims.claim: The speaker believes Uber faces significant risks from autonomous vehicle competition and does not see a great long-term outcome for the ride-hailing business.
claims.quote: I don't really see a great scenario for Uber here. Honestly I mean what's a great outcome in the ride hailing market for Uber in the next 10 years they're not gonna sit on top of all these AV cumodles, that's not an outcome. I just don't rate that.

claims.claim: The speaker argues that Uber will benefit from AVs by acting as an aggregator, maintaining high market share, and leveraging operating leverage to improve margins.
claims.quote: So you could say the market expands a lot because AVs are a lot cheaper than ride hail so eventually the price of rides goes down and even if there is these two other players Uber still has a huge portion of this market share that's much higher and absolute dollars than it currently is today.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests Uber could achieve a 30% margin business if they don't have to promote to defend their turf, supported by loyalty programs and the Uber Eats business.
claims.quote: you know maybe they take this to a 30% margin business which doesn't seem crazy if they don't have to promote and defend their turf and so you have a lot higher usage with operating leverage giving them higher margin

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Uber currently has a 14.5% margin and has enjoyed operating leverage in recent years.
claims.quote: but they're still only at a 14 and a half percent margin you know maybe they take this to a 30% margin business

claims.claim: The speaker acknowledges Uber won the rideshare wars but notes that new competition from autonomous vehicle providers could ultimately weigh on profitability.
claims.quote: I do think that there's a way out for them that they end up being a fine business and that is that there are a lot of autonomous vehicle providers so we know that there's Zeus already we know that Lucid and Nuro are teaming up

claims.claim: The speaker questions how Uber can compete with Waymo on cost and notes that Waymo's lower variable costs might lead to more aggressive promotion and discounting.
claims.quote: I mean from a cost standpoint though how can Uber ever compete with Waymo? If the again the density of their cars are significant enough clearly of a Waymo is 20 minutes away or something of that nature

claims.claim: The speaker states that promoting rides for Uber often eats into margin due to high variable costs associated with driver payouts.
claims.quote: whereas when Uber promotes because of their higher variable cost very often promoting actually eats into margin and we saw that prior.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Uber's food delivery app and loyalty program help retain users who are less likely to switch between different AV providers.
claims.quote: and then you also have kind of the benefit of the Uber Eats business and the loyalty program and those two together mean that people that use Uber tend to be more loyal users, they retain longer

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Uber's advertising business continues to improve and they have entered the hotel business.
claims.quote: and it's also worth pointing out that the Uber Eats business has different competitive dynamics than the ride hail business because when you are dealing with restaurants it's a very fragmented base

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that Google's dominance in restaurant search could potentially impact food delivery, though they find that scenario far-fetched.
claims.quote: So maybe that is a like into food delivery using waymos and robots and such. So I don't know about that one. That one seems a little more far fetched but it doesn't seem impossible either.
